newsitem.title: UK: CSFB warns on Slovak current account,credit rating.
newsitem.headline: CSFB warns on Slovak current account,credit rating.

text.p: The Slovak authorities will have to act rapidly to prevent further deterioration in the country's current account deficit and protect the country's investment grade rating, CS First Boston economist Istvan Racz said in a research report.
Slovakia's current account has swung from a $649 million surplus in 1995 to an expected $1.4 billion deficit this year, or 7.9 percent of gross domestic product.
"The authorities will have to step up adjustement efforts in 1997 in order to protect the country's investment grade borrower status," Racz said.
He believes that the key consequence of the deterioration in the deficit is that the deficit will exceed 10 percent of GDP in 1997.

"Even though external debt is relatively low - $6.34 billion or 33.2 percent of GDP in September 1996 - and currency reserves are high ($4.8 billion), it is not at all likely that Slovakia could sustain its investment grade borrowing status with a current account above this level and growing," Racz said.
He said the government will have to accelerate reforms to halt the deterioration, especially privatisation and the overhaul of the fiscal sector.

The National Bank has substantially tightened monetary policy and money market rates are now an annualised 13.5-14.0 percent compared with 5.3 percent in October, helping to cut inflation from 7.2 percent at end-1995 to 5.3 percent in October.

This has also had an impact on growth, with industrial production growth falling to 2.8 percent in the first nine months of this year from 8.3 percent in 1995. The government also faces a dilemma on devaluation, between domestic price stability and declining GDP.

"The current evidence suggests that the government is not ready to devalue. However, the projected trend of the external balance shows that their policy mix wil have to be reconsidered - probably including devaluation - in the second half of 1997.
